messages.author: 3d7541308bd2e290
messages.subject: Using external software inside Stan
parts:
I think this question has been asked a lot, but I wanted to clarify.

I've got a small custom HMC code that does Bayesian inference for a structural mechanics problem.

I'd like to do inferences on it in Stan so I can take advantage of the Stan samplers and use the Stan modeling language for the priors and stuff. However:

1. The problem, at the end of the day, reduces to a big eigenvalue solve. I need control over the eigenvalue solve beyond what Stan currently offers (generalized eigenvalue solve, only need the few smallest eigenvalues)

2. The actual mechanics are kinda black box too. I could conceivably code up some of the matrix assembly stuff in Stan, but it isn't terribly practical, and in the near future I might be needing some other software to do the assembly for me anyway.

Either way, I can provide my stuff as a black box. So it takes in parameters, and spits out some stuff that corresponds roughly to data I'm measuring. I can also provide the gradients for this as well.

So if I want to implement the 'mechanics_solve' thing in something like:

data ~ normal(mechanics_solve(parameters), sigma);

And I have my forward function evaluation as well as my gradients, where's the best place for me to start? I use PyStan, if that changes anything.

From what I've dug up on the mailing list, I go here: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan, find a function that looks reasonably like what I want in the Stan Math library, and plug away?

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using external software inside Stan
parts:
If you can write up a C++ function that does what you want,
then we can help you plug it together. If you have analytic
gradients, you can just plug them in using:

stan_math/stan/math/rev/core/stored_gradient_vari.hpp

That is, you want your function to be something like this:

std::vector<var> mechanics_solve(const std::vector<var>& v) {
copy args into double structure
compute values and gradients
use stored_gradient_vari to create return vars
return them
}

You need to use our built in allocation memalloc_.allocate_array<T>(size)
to generate the pointer arrays to pass into the stored gradients so
there are no memory leaks.

I should write this up in the how to write functions.

Then just add it to symbol table and you're good to go (assuming you
can build it into PyStan or use it from CmdStan).

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Using external software inside Stan
parts:
On Monday, March 13, 2017 at 6:32:36 PM UTC-4, Ben B wrote:
1. The problem, at the end of the day, reduces to a big eigenvalue solve. I need control over the eigenvalue solve beyond what Stan currently offers (generalized eigenvalue solve, only need the few smallest eigenvalues)

Stan cannot autodiff through complex generalized eigenvalues, which is why we currently only support eigenvalues of symmetric matrices. Even if your small eigenvalues happen to be real, if complex arithmetic is used, it will probably segfault. I have some stuff on a branch that mitigates some of these problems using what Eigen calls a pseudo-eigendecomposition that only uses real arithmetic but it doesn't do anything partial like finding the few smallest generalized pseudo-eigenvalues.

Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using external software inside Stan
parts:
On Tuesday, March 14, 2017 at 12:17:39 PM UTC-4, Ben B wrote:
@BGoodrich

Yeah, the eigenvalues are actually real in this problem. I'm pretty sure something in ARPACK will solve my problem (I think that's what Scipy uses under the hood anyway?) -- it's just a matter of knocking the dust off my documentation reading skills.

The eigenvalues not only need to be real; the C++ needs to use real arithmetic exclusively to calculate them. If it is using complex<T> then you are going to have pull the double values out of the stan::math::var types, calculate the small eigenvalues, do the derivatives analytically, and then attach the derivatives to new stan::math::var values. And that is a lot of work.

The function signature I settled on was:

void mechanics(double c11, double anisotropic, double c44, // These are the parameters I want to estimate for now
               Eigen::Tensor<double, 4> *dp, Eigen::Tensor<double, 2> *pv, unsigned int nevs, // These are constant bits of data I can initialize and pass into Stan in as vectors or whatever
               MatrixXd **freqs,  // This is the output -- an (nevs x 1) matrix of eigenvalues
               MatrixXd **dfreqs_dc11 = NULL, MatrixXd **dfreqs_da = NULL, MatrixXd **dfreqs_dc44 = NULL) // This is output too -- these are the derivatives of the eigenvalues wrt the parameters

What's the closest thing in the Stan Math library to this (for me to start working on)? I can rearrange things so the input is just a vector and output is just a vector (like you showed in your original e-mail), but for testing I thought this was cleaner. What do I need to do about the constants (the things I won't need to differentiate with respect to)?

I attached a little PDF with some details about the problem as well as the rough Stan model I'd like to write. If the attachment doesn't work, it's available here: https://www.overleaf.com/read/qpcmfzmxfxsf

Basically all the code that I'd need hook up to the Stan Math library is here: https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/mechanics.hpp and https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/polybasis.hpp . The only super necessary external dependency for now is LAPACK.

There's a really simple sampler here (from the 2012 Radford Neal paper) that I tested things with: https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/main.cpp . I've got traceplots from that, if anyone is curious.

@Michael, yeah, we're all pretty curious over here to see what NUTS thinks of the problem. It would be nice to not have to guess and check with timesteps a bunch to get the the thing sampling efficiently too.

Thanks a lot!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using external software inside Stan
parts:
This should all be OK if you're writing a function for
your own use and can deal with the LAPACK linkage. Our
existing functions tend to be much more C++ oriented, with
constant reference arguments and return values; under the hood
we sometimes work with raw pointers when we need to control our
own memory.

Basically, you need to be able to construct the vari objects
that correspond to your results with chain() methods that do
the reverse mode autodiff (multiply the function's result's
adjoints by the partials and add to the corresponding operand's
adjoints). This is all explained in our arXiv paper.

If you just want an example of multivariate functions, all
of the matrix functions are like this, but their code's pretty
involved.

For constants (double arguments, presumably), you don't need
to do anything. You won't be able to run Stan programs
that deal with them as parameters, but you shouldn't need to.
We don't have built-in functions like that.

- Bob

On Tue, Mar 28, 2017 at 9:19 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

This should all be OK if you're writing a function for
your own use and can deal with the LAPACK linkage.  Our
existing functions tend to be much more C++ oriented, with
constant reference arguments and return values;  under the hood
we sometimes work with raw pointers when we need to control our
own memory.

Basically, you need to be able to construct the vari objects
that correspond to your results with chain() methods that do
the reverse mode autodiff (multiply the function's result's
adjoints by the partials and add to the corresponding operand's
adjoints). This is all explained in our arXiv paper.

If you just want an example of multivariate functions, all
of the matrix functions are like this, but their code's pretty
involved.

For constants (double arguments, presumably), you don't need
to do anything.  You won't be able to run Stan programs
that deal with them as parameters, but you shouldn't need to.
We don't have built-in functions like that.

- Bob

It's party hat time!

Got a really simple exampled coded up (using the cmdStan stuff BGoodrich recommended). Here's the direct comparison from what I had to Stan (model here: https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/test.stan):

Parameter     HMC (100 samples)  Stan (100 samples), posteriors shown as mean +- 1 standard deviation
c11           1.7 +- 0.019       1.7 +- 0.017
a             1.0 +- 0.0024      1.0 +- 0.0024
c44           0.45 +- 0.00078    0.45 +- 0.0007
sigma         0.43 +- 0.062      0.44 +- 0.069

I told Gmail to use a fixed space font so hopefully that worked.

I'll need to add a few things to put the full mechanics model in and test some harder problems (and see if I can get away without the guesses) but it looks like we have liftoff!

Does NUTS use the 2nd version (the non-var specialization)? I added some debug print statements and it looks like the variational inference code uses it.

I'll follow up again after I've done more tests and attach a write up.

Thanks folks! This is gonna be super useful.

Does NUTS use the 2nd version (the non-var specialization)? I added some debug print statements and it looks like the variational inference code uses it.

I'll follow up again after I've done more tests and attach a write up.

Thanks folks! This is gonna be super useful.

Ben
